title: Why stealing an authorization code is not enough
answer: Redeeming the code also needs the verifier, which never passes through the redirect

checks.question: Why does the app not embed one fixed client secret in its program and send that with the token request instead?
checks.answer: Every installed copy carries the same secret, so anyone can extract it from the program, including the author of the malicious app, and the server could not tell the copies apart. The verifier is made fresh for each sign-in and stays on the device until the client’s own TLS request.

checks.question: Suppose the malicious app can also read the authorization request, so it holds the challenge E9Melh… as well as the code. Can it now redeem the code?
checks.answer: No. The server wants a verifier whose S256 equals the challenge. Knowing the challenge does not produce such a verifier: finding one for a verifier made from 32 random bytes is computationally infeasible, so whatever the app sends still gets invalid_grant.

checks.question: RFC 7636 also defines a plain method, in which the challenge is the verifier itself. Against the app in the previous question, what changes?
checks.answer: It succeeds. The challenge it read is the verifier, so it can present the code with that verifier and get a token. Plain protects only when the authorization request itself cannot be read, which is why RFC 7636 requires clients that can use S256 to use it (§4.2, §7.2).

scenarios.name: Replay the theft against PKCE: Yes
invariants: a code bound to a challenge gives the malicious app no token

steps.title: Another app can catch the redirect and redeem its code
steps.line: Predict: the thief has the code and public request fields. What could stop it?
steps.caption: A mobile or desktop app often gets its authorization code back as a redirect to a custom URI scheme. Another app on the device can register the same scheme, and the operating system may hand it the redirect and its code (RFC 7636 §1). This public client has no client secret. The thief knows the ordinary token-request fields, such as the client ID and redirect URI, so presenting the stolen code gets it an access token in this unprotected exchange.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 5 messages. Note: “a token for the wrong app” beside Auth server → Malicious app: Access token; theft: Auth server → Malicious app: Redirect via the shared URI scheme; Malicious app → Auth server: Token request: code; Auth server → Malicious app: Access token.

steps.title: Answer: bind the code to a secret the real client keeps
steps.line: The challenge is the base64url SHA-256 of the verifier.
steps.caption: A fixed secret shipped inside the app could be extracted from any copy, so for each sign-in the client makes a fresh random code_verifier and keeps it. Ahead of the redirect it sends the code_challenge instead: the verifier’s SHA-256 in base64url, a method called S256. Redeeming the code also needs the verifier, which never passes through the redirect. The server stores the challenge now and recognizes the right verifier later without having seen it. This is PKCE, Proof Key for Code Exchange; the card uses RFC 7636’s example verifier.
steps.picture: Flowchart: 3 nodes, 2 links; 3 labelled values. Travelled: code_verifier → 32-byte digest: SHA-256; 32-byte digest → code_challenge: base64url; marked: code_challenge; code_challenge: E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM.

steps.title: The authorization request carries the challenge and S256
steps.line: It goes through the browser, so treat the challenge as public.
steps.caption: The client sends the challenge and the S256 method in the authorization request, through the user’s browser. The challenge is treated as public; the verifier stays with the client and is not sent. The user then signs in and consents at the auth server.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 1 message. Note: “challenge + S256; verifier not sent” beside Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge.

steps.title: The redirect carries a short-lived code bound to the challenge
steps.line: Predict: the malicious app catches this code again. What happens when it redeems it?
steps.caption: The server stores the challenge with a short-lived code and redirects the browser back to the client. Because the verifier has not travelled, an app that catches this redirect gets the code and nothing else, and the code still has to be exchanged for an access token.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 2 messages. Note: “code bound to the challenge” beside Auth server → Client: Redirect with code; carries the code: Auth server → Client: Redirect with code; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge.

steps.title: Answer: invalid_grant. The stolen code fails without the verifier
steps.line: S256 of the guess differs from the challenge bound to the code.
steps.caption: The malicious app catches the redirect and its code as before, but the token request now needs a verifier. Lacking it, the app sends a guess. The server computes S256 of the guess, compares it with the challenge stored with the code, finds they differ and answers invalid_grant. The note shows six characters of each; the server compares the whole value.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 5 messages. Attack: Auth server → Malicious app: Redirect via the shared URI scheme; Malicious app → Auth server: Token request: code + a guess; Auth server → Malicious app: invalid_grant; note: “S256(guess) = X4OLkc… ≠ E9Melh…” beside Auth server → Malicious app: invalid_grant; and 2 more.

steps.title: The real client redeems the code: S256 of its verifier matches
steps.line: The calculation that rejected the guess now finds equal values.
steps.caption: The real client sends the code with the verifier it kept. The server computes S256 of the verifier, finds that it equals the challenge stored with the code, and returns an access token, provided its usual checks on the code and the client also pass.
steps.picture: Sequence diagram: 3 participants, 7 messages. Accepted: Client → Auth server: Token request: code + code_verifier; Auth server → Client: Access token; note: “S256(verifier) = E9Melh… = bound challenge” beside Auth server → Client: Access token; carries the challenge: Client → Auth server: Authorize request + code_challenge; and 4 more.

steps.title: The code crosses the browser; the verifier does not
steps.line: Red lane: what another app can read. Green: the client’s own TLS.
steps.caption: Drawn by channel instead of by time, the client’s sign-in uses two routes. The challenge and the code pass through the browser and the operating system’s redirect, the red lane, where another app can read them. The verifier, made from 32 random bytes, goes only in the client’s own TLS request to the token endpoint, the green lane, together with the code. Reading the challenge does not help a thief, because finding a verifier whose S256 equals it is computationally infeasible. The protection lasts while the verifier stays secret: an attacker who can read the app’s memory gets the verifier as well as the code, and the server can no longer tell the two apps apart.
steps.picture: Two lanes between the client on the left and the auth server on the right. The red, dashed lane is the browser and the redirect, which another app can read: Client to Auth server, code_challenge and code_challenge_method; Auth server to Client, code. The green lane is the client’s own TLS connection to the token endpoint: Client to Auth server, code and code_verifier; Auth server to Client, access token. Another app can read code_challenge, code_challenge_method and code, and not the code_verifier.

steps.title: Even redeemed first, the stolen code gets invalid_grant
steps.line: The malicious app catches the redirect first and redeems before the client has the code.
steps.caption: Here the malicious app catches the redirect before the client does and sends its token request at once. The server compares S256 of its guess with the challenge stored with the code and answers invalid_grant; in this model the refusal leaves the code unused, so the client’s request with the verifier still gets the token. While the authorization request carries the challenge, in every order of these messages the malicious app never gets a token. Without the challenge, whichever app redeems first gets it, and the other gets invalid_grant, because a code is used once.
steps.picture: Three lifelines, the client, the auth server and the malicious app, across a red dashed browser lane other apps can read and a green TLS lane. Browser lane: Client to Auth server, code_challenge (S256). Browser lane: Auth server to Client, code. Browser lane: Auth server to Malicious app, code. TLS lane: Client to Auth server, code + code_verifier. TLS lane: Malicious app to Auth server, code + a guess. TLS lane: Auth server to Client, Access token. TLS lane: Auth server to Malicious app, invalid_grant (S256(guess) ≠ challenge). Under Client: keeps code_verifier. Under Auth server: stores the challenge · code used.
